articles.title: Vishal Sikka Ran Infosys. Now He's Built an AI Startup Aimed at Killing the Business He Came From.
articles.excerpt: The former Infosys CEO's new venture, Hang Ten Systems, raised $32 million to let AI do the integration-and-maintenance grunt work that built India's $315 billion IT industry.
articles.image_caption: Vishal Sikka, former CEO of Infosys, speaking at an enterprise technology conference.
articles.nri_angle: Hundreds of thousands of Indian engineers — in Bengaluru delivery centers and on H-1B and L-1 visas at US client sites — earn a living doing exactly the integration and maintenance work Sikka now wants software to automate.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Washington Just Cut Off Foreign Nationals From Anthropic's Best AI. India's 'Sovereign AI' Startups Got the Gift of the Year.
articles.excerpt: A US export-control order barring all foreign nationals — even Anthropic's own employees — from its top models has made the case for homegrown AI overnight. Sarvam and a wave of Indian builders are the unexpected winners.
articles.image_caption: Server racks in a secure data center, the infrastructure layer at the heart of the sovereign-AI debate.
articles.nri_angle: Indian engineers and founders building or relying on frontier AI just watched access to the best US model get revoked in 90 minutes — proof that for NRIs and India alike, depending on a single foreign lab is now a strategic risk, not a convenience.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's IT Giants Just Lost ₹8.5 Lakh Crore in Five Years. The Companies Replacing Them on the Value Charts Are AI Startups.
articles.excerpt: TCS, Infosys, and Wipro are the only major Indian sector to post a cumulative decline in value — while four pure-play AI firms, led by Sarvam, crashed onto the rankings. For NRI investors, the great rotation is here.
articles.image_caption: A financial trading screen displaying market charts and data.
articles.nri_angle: NRIs hold Indian IT through mutual funds, ADRs, and direct stakes as the safe, dividend-paying bet on India's tech story — but the value is rotating from the outsourcers their generation worked for to the AI startups disrupting them.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's First Private Rocket-to-Orbit Is on the Pad. The Company Behind It Isn't ISRO.
articles.excerpt: Skyroot's Vikram-1 is in final preparations at Sriharikota for the maiden orbital flight of an Indian private rocket — backed by GIC, BlackRock and an early Google investor.
articles.image_caption: Skyroot Aerospace's Vikram-S rocket lifts off on Mission Prarambh from Sriharikota in November 2022, India's first private rocket to reach space.
articles.nri_angle: For NRI investors eyeing India's marquee IPOs and for diaspora aerospace engineers weighing a move home, Skyroot's launch is proof that India now has a private space economy — not just a state space programme.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Just Set Its Chip Budget for the Year: Rs 7,100 Crore, and a Quiet Bet on Design Over Fabs
articles.excerpt: The FY27 plan funds one fab, nine manufacturing units and thirty design firms — an admission that India will compete where its engineers already dominate, not where Taiwan does.
articles.image_caption: A 200mm semiconductor wafer fabrication line, the kind of back-end and manufacturing capacity India's FY27 incentives target.
articles.nri_angle: For the Indian-origin chip engineer at Nvidia or Qualcomm, India's design-led semiconductor bet is the clearest 'you could do this at home' signal yet — aimed at exactly the work the diaspora already dominates abroad.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Oracle Just Told the SEC That AI Cost 21,000 Jobs. India Took More Than Half of Them.
articles.excerpt: The most candid admission yet that AI is replacing tech workers came in a regulatory filing — and roughly 12,000 of the cuts landed in India, where Oracle's largest workforce sits.
articles.image_caption: Oracle, which told the SEC that AI adoption contributed to cutting about 21,000 jobs (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Oracle is the first major tech firm to put AI job losses in writing to regulators, and with India absorbing the largest share, it is a warning shot for every Indian engineer on an H-1B watching the same companies spend on data centers while thinning their ranks.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Got Its First 'Sovereign AI' Unicorn. The Twist Is Who Wrote the Biggest Cheque.
articles.excerpt: Bengaluru's Sarvam AI raised $234 million at a $1.5 billion valuation — but the lead investor was not a global VC. It was HCLTech, an Indian IT giant betting $150 million on homegrown models.
articles.image_caption: HCLTech led the funding round in Sarvam AI, India's first 'sovereign AI' unicorn (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Sarvam's round is the clearest sign yet that India intends to build its own AI stack rather than rent one from Silicon Valley — a shift that reshapes where diaspora engineers and NRI investors place their bets on the next decade of Indian tech.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Nvidia Gets the Headlines. But an Indian-Origin CEO Sells the One Chip AI Data Centers Can't Run Without.
articles.excerpt: SiTime, led by Rajesh Vashist, makes the timing chips that keep AI clusters in sync. Revenue jumped 88%, the stock has roughly tripled this year, and inference may need four times more of its product.
articles.image_caption: A close-up of a motherboard and microchips, the kind of precision components SiTime designs for AI data centers
articles.nri_angle: While the diaspora obsesses over Nvidia, an Indian-origin CEO is quietly riding the same AI wave from an unglamorous corner of the chip stack — a reminder that the semiconductor boom NRI investors and engineers are tracking runs far deeper than GPUs.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Credit-Card Rewards Founder From Bengaluru Just Got Handed WhatsApp's 3 Billion Users
articles.excerpt: Meta is putting $900 million into CRED and naming Kunal Shah as WhatsApp's first Indian chief. The diaspora's most-used app now answers to a man who built his name on getting Indians to pay their bills on time.
articles.image_caption: Kunal Shah, founder of CRED and FreeCharge, now appointed global head of WhatsApp
articles.nri_angle: WhatsApp is the connective tissue of the Indian diaspora — the app NRIs use to call parents in Pune and run side businesses in New Jersey — and it will now be steered by an Indian founder whose payments instincts point the monetization experiments straight at India first.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Hackers Put Apple and Tesla Trade Secrets on the Dark Web. The Leak Came From a Tata Plant in Tamil Nadu.
articles.excerpt: A ransomware crew claims to have lifted iPhone inspection manuals and Tesla part drawings from Tata Electronics, the company carrying India's bet that it can build the West's gadgets. The breach lands as India races to become Apple's factory floor.
articles.image_caption: Tata Electronics, the Tata Group arm that assembles iPhones in India, suffered a data breach (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: The 'Made in India' iPhone in an NRI's pocket depends on Tata's Tamil Nadu plants staying secure and trusted; a breach exposing Apple and Tesla secrets is a direct test of whether India can be the world's trusted manufacturing base, not just its cheapest one.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Promised Chips for Years. By November, a Tata Plant in Assam Says It Will Actually Ship 48 Million of Them.
articles.excerpt: A state once defined by insurgency is about to become a semiconductor exporter. For a diaspora that has watched India announce fabs and miss deadlines, a concrete shipping date is the news.
articles.image_caption: Tata Semiconductor's Assam ATMP plant aims to begin exporting packaged chips by November (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Semiconductor professionals in the diaspora have heard India's chip promises before; the first real export volumes out of Assam are the proof point that decides whether 'return to India' is a serious career bet or still aspirational.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: UPI Was Built So Indians Could Split a Dinner Bill. It Just Went Live at a Paris Department Store.
articles.excerpt: India's payments rail now works in eleven countries, from the Eiffel Tower to a Cambodian street market. For the diaspora, the home-screen app is quietly becoming a passport.
articles.image_caption: A shopper makes a contactless QR-code payment with a smartphone, the everyday gesture UPI is now exporting abroad.
articles.nri_angle: NRIs who fly home no longer need to juggle forex cards or cash across nine-plus countries — the same UPI app on their phone now pays merchants from Paris to Phnom Penh, and the corridor map is expanding toward the markets where the diaspora actually lives.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: An Indian-Born CEO Now Supplies the Memory for Claude — and Has Bought a Slice of the Company That Builds It.
articles.excerpt: Micron's deal with Anthropic ties Sanjay Mehrotra's memory empire directly to a frontier AI lab, days before an earnings report that could show a tenfold jump in profit.
articles.image_caption: A green memory module on a circuit board — the high-bandwidth memory at the centre of the AI build-out.
articles.nri_angle: For NRI investors holding Micron and for the thousands of Indian engineers inside the memory and AI-infrastructure supply chain, the Anthropic pact is a signal that the chip cycle that funds their RSUs has shifted from boom-and-bust to a structural AI build-out — with an Indian-American CEO sitting at the chokepoint.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Cognizant Just Wired ServiceNow's AI Agents Into Its Own. The Indian IT Workforce Is the Experiment.
articles.excerpt: An open-source 'agent orchestrator' lets one company's bots talk to another's. For the millions who staff India's services industry, it is a preview of the job that is being automated.
articles.image_caption: Cognizant Technology Solutions via flickr (BY-SA)
articles.nri_angle: Cognizant employs hundreds of thousands of Indians and is a top sponsor of H-1B workers in the US; its push to make AI agents do cross-platform enterprise work is a direct signal to NRI techies in IT services about which roles get automated first — and which become more valuable.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Wall Street Asked If Arista's AI Boom Was Over. Jayshree Ullal Just Lifted the Bet to 1.6 Terabits.
articles.excerpt: Arista Networks grew revenue 35% to $2.7 billion as hyperscalers wired their AI data centres with its switches. The Indian-origin CEO is now selling the plumbing for the next wave.
articles.image_caption: Jayshree Ullal, chairperson and CEO of Arista Networks
articles.nri_angle: Arista is one of Silicon Valley's quietest wealth machines for Indian-American engineers and investors, and its fortunes now ride entirely on whether the AI data-centre build-out keeps going.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Every IT Firm Says AI Will Shrink Its Workforce. At Infosys's AGM, Nandan Nilekani Said the Opposite.
articles.excerpt: Infosys sees a $300-400 billion AI-services market by decade's end and plans to keep hiring 20,000 freshers a year — a sharp break from the layoff narrative gripping the rest of tech.
articles.image_caption: Nandan Nilekani, co-founder and chairman of Infosys
articles.nri_angle: For the millions of Indians and NRIs whose careers run through Infosys and its peers, the company is making the contrarian case that AI is a tailwind for IT services jobs, not their executioner.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: For 30 Years India Guarded Its Workhorse Rocket. It Just Decided to Hand the Keys to Private Firms.
articles.excerpt: IN-SPACe has invited private companies to take over the PSLV — the rocket that launched Chandrayaan and 104 satellites at once. Only Indian-controlled firms qualify.
articles.image_caption: An ISRO PSLV rocket lifts off from Sriharikota
articles.nri_angle: India's privatising space sector is opening up to NRI capital and returning engineers just as the global small-satellite launch market explodes — but the Indian-ownership rule sets clear terms for who can play.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: An Indian-Born CEO Out-Earned Tim Cook and Satya Nadella. His Own Shareholders Have Voted No Seven Times.
articles.excerpt: Nikesh Arora's roughly $100 million package put him among the S&P 500's highest-paid bosses. The fight over whether he's worth it is a window into how the diaspora's corner-office generation is now judged.
articles.image_caption: Nikesh Arora, CEO of Palo Alto Networks, speaking at TechCrunch Disrupt
articles.nri_angle: Indian-origin executives now run some of America's most valuable companies; how shareholders judge their pay versus their performance sets the template for the next generation of NRI leaders climbing the corporate ladder.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Qualcomm Spent Two Decades Selling Phone Chips. In a Single Month It Has Bid Up to $14 Billion to Escape Them.
articles.excerpt: Back-to-back talks to buy Modular and Tenstorrent are Qualcomm's bid to crash Nvidia's data-center party — and a fresh battleground for the Indian engineers who design these chips.
articles.image_caption: Tower servers in a data center, the market Qualcomm is racing to enter with a pair of AI acquisitions
articles.nri_angle: Qualcomm's pivot from handsets to AI data centers is creating a new tier of high-value silicon and software jobs in San Diego and the Bay Area — the kind of roles Indian-American chip designers and ML-infrastructure engineers are positioned to fill.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: An Indian IT Giant Just Won the Job of Running a US Chipmaker's Computers. The Twist Is What's Replacing the Humans.
articles.excerpt: Infosys expanded its GlobalFoundries deal to run the chipmaker's entire enterprise IT on AI and automation — a glimpse of how India's outsourcing model is reinventing itself, and what it means for the engineers inside it.
articles.image_caption: Close-up of a computer processor; Infosys will run GlobalFoundries' enterprise IT under a new AI-led contract
articles.nri_angle: Indian IT services firms employ tens of thousands of NRIs in the US; the shift from people-heavy outsourcing to AI-run 'managed services' decides whose jobs survive and which skills now command a premium.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Nvidia and Azim Premji Just Bet $190 Million on AI's Least Glamorous Problem. The Founders Are Indian-American.
articles.excerpt: Upscale AI, run by serial diaspora entrepreneurs, hit a $2 billion valuation building the networking 'plumbing' that connects AI chips — funded by Indian money and Silicon Valley's biggest names.
articles.image_caption: Azim Premji, whose Premji Invest led Upscale AI's $190 million funding round (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Indian-origin serial founders, backed by Azim Premji's investment arm and Nvidia, are building the AI networking layer in Palo Alto — a signal for NRI engineers weighing infrastructure startups and investors tracking cross-border Indian capital into frontier American tech.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Can't Out-Build Taiwan's Chip Fabs. So It's Betting It Can Out-Design Everyone.
articles.excerpt: With Indians already 20% of the world's chip-design workforce, New Delhi is targeting a million-strong global talent shortage — and the diaspora is its most underused asset.
articles.image_caption: Indian IT and Electronics Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw
articles.nri_angle: India's pivot from fabs to chip design reshapes the career map for the huge cohort of NRI engineers at Nvidia, Qualcomm, Intel and Micron — creating return-to-India and investment options, and positioning India as a neutral design hub amid US-China chip tensions.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Satya Nadella Spent a Decade Cheering AI On. Now He Wants the Industry to Slow Its Own Hype.
articles.excerpt: Microsoft's chief executive is warning that AI power is dangerously concentrated — and quietly opening Azure to cheaper models, including China's DeepSeek, to break the logjam.
articles.image_caption: Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella, who is pressing the AI industry to spread its gains more widely.
articles.nri_angle: For the tens of thousands of Indian engineers inside Microsoft and its enterprise customers, Nadella's pivot from a single-model bet to a multi-model marketplace decides whose AI skills stay in demand and whose roles get automated first.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Micron Is About to Post a 1,000% Profit Jump. The Indian-Born CEO Behind It Is Sitting on a Memory Shortage With No End in Sight.
articles.excerpt: Sanjay Mehrotra's company has become one of the AI boom's biggest winners — its high-bandwidth memory sold out through 2026 — as it builds a fab in Gujarat that could anchor India's chip ambitions.
articles.image_caption: Micron chief executive Sanjay Mehrotra, who is steering the memory maker through an AI-driven supply crunch.
articles.nri_angle: Micron is the rare AI trade that connects an NRI investor's brokerage account to Modi's semiconductor push — its Gujarat plant is India's first major memory facility, and its stock has become a diaspora favorite for betting on the chip supercycle.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Just Shipped $2.4 Billion of Phones to America in a Single Month. Apple Is Carrying Almost All of It.
articles.excerpt: Smartphone exports to the US jumped 47% in April even after India lost its tariff edge over China — and Trump is openly pressuring Tim Cook to build at home instead.
articles.image_caption: Apple's iPhone, now by value India's single largest branded export to the United States (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Every iPhone an NRI buys in the US is now likely assembled in Tamil Nadu or Karnataka, turning India into a load-bearing pillar of Apple's supply chain — and a flashpoint in the US-India trade fight that could reshape diaspora business ties.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's Quietest AI Investor Just Showed Its Hand: Rs 1,003 Crore Across 54 Startups
articles.excerpt: Info Edge, the firm behind Naukri and an early Zomato backer, carved out its AI and deeptech bets as a separate book for the first time — and was unusually frank about how few have paid off yet.
articles.image_caption: Early-stage technology startups of the kind Info Edge's deeptech funds back (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: For NRIs who treat Info Edge as a proxy for India's internet economy, the disclosure is a rare honest map of where smart Indian capital is betting on AI — and a reminder that the deeptech wave is still years from returns.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Bengaluru Startup Wants to Build India's Largest Security Operations Centre. Bessemer Just Bet $15 Million on It.
articles.excerpt: Mitigata raised a Series B less than a year after its last round, betting that AI-driven attacks and a chronic talent shortage have created a 'perfect storm' for Indian enterprises.
articles.image_caption: A data centre; the kind of monitoring infrastructure cyber-resilience firms run around the clock (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: NRIs increasingly hold accounts, run businesses and store data with Indian banks and firms — the institutions Mitigata is racing to protect — making India's cyber-resilience build-out a direct concern for the diaspora, not a distant domestic story.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Has a New Real-Estate Unicorn. The Twist Is How It Got There — and Who's Buying.
articles.excerpt: Square Yards crossed a $1 billion valuation on a Rs 900 crore debt-and-equity round, riding a property platform built in no small part on the wallets of non-resident Indians.
articles.image_caption: Residential buildings in India; the property sector has minted a new unicorn (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Square Yards built its business partly by selling Indian property to NRIs — so its rise to unicorn status is, in a literal sense, a story about where the diaspora's money has been going.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Razorpay Came Home to India, Then Quietly Filed to Go Public. The Reverse-Flip Era Has Its Marquee Test.
articles.excerpt: The payments giant filed confidential IPO papers with SEBI, seeking up to $700 million at a valuation reset to $5-6 billion. After a costly move from Delaware back to Bengaluru, its listing is a referendum on whether Indian startups belong on Indian exchanges.
articles.image_caption: The Bombay Stock Exchange building on Dalal Street, Mumbai. Razorpay has filed confidential IPO papers with SEBI, aiming for a main-board listing on India's exchanges.
articles.nri_angle: For NRIs who built or backed Indian startups through US holding structures, Razorpay's expensive journey home and its listing on an Indian exchange is the clearest signal yet that the centre of gravity for Indian tech value creation has shifted from Delaware and Nasdaq back to Bengaluru and Dalal Street.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: An AI That Refuses to Answer Until It Can Prove It Is Right. IIT Madras Alumni Just Raised $27 Million to Build It.
articles.excerpt: Pramaana Labs, backed by Vinod Khosla, is wrapping large language models in mathematical proof engines so AI can be trusted in tax, law and medicine. Half its team sits in India — a bet that the next AI breakthrough is reliability, not raw intelligence.
articles.image_caption: Vinod Khosla, whose firm Khosla Ventures led Pramaana Labs' $27 million seed round. The Indian-American venture capitalist was an early backer of OpenAI.
articles.nri_angle: Founded by IIT Madras alumni with half its workforce in India and led by a round from Indian-American legend Vinod Khosla, Pramaana embodies the US-India deep-tech bridge: the hardest problems in AI being attacked by Indian engineering talent on both sides of the Pacific.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Swiggy Rider Can Now Start a Mutual Fund in a Few Taps. India Just Wired Investing Into the Gig Economy.
articles.excerpt: Swiggy's tie-up with Zerodha Fund House lets delivery partners invest from Rs 100 straight through their rider app. It is a small feature with a big idea behind it — formal finance reaching the people the formal economy usually skips.
articles.image_caption: A Swiggy delivery partner on the road in India. Riders can now invest part of their earnings in mutual funds through the same app they use for deliveries.
articles.nri_angle: For NRIs who hold Swiggy stock or watch India's fintech rails, this is a live test of whether digital public infrastructure can pull millions of informal workers into formal investing — the next frontier after UPI moved money and Aadhaar moved identity.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Foreign Satellite Giants Are Stuck at India's Door. Mukesh Ambani Just Decided to Build His Own Constellation.
articles.excerpt: As Starlink and Amazon wait on Delhi's security clearances, Jio says it will build a sovereign low-Earth-orbit network for India — a bet that connectivity from space should be Indian-owned.
articles.image_caption: An artist's impression of a low-Earth-orbit satellite constellation. Jio says it will build a sovereign LEO network for India.
articles.nri_angle: NRIs who send devices, money and expectations of connectivity back to rural India have a direct stake in who controls the satellite broadband that finally reaches the village — a foreign operator on a licence, or a sovereign Indian network built to stay.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Indians Are Putting Solar on the Roof Faster Than Anyone Expected. Investors Just Poured Rs 510 Crore Into the Company Riding That Wave.
articles.excerpt: SolarSquare's new funding round, led by Lightspeed, is a bet that rooftop solar has crossed from subsidy story to consumer habit — powered by the PM Surya Ghar scheme and rising electricity bills.
articles.image_caption: Rooftop solar panels on homes in Mehsana, Gujarat. India's residential solar market is drawing major venture capital.
articles.nri_angle: For NRIs funding solar panels on the family home back in India, or eyeing the country's clean-energy boom as an investment, SolarSquare's raise marks the moment rooftop solar stopped being a green gesture and became a mainstream consumer purchase.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Just Approved Its First Silicon-Carbide Fab. The Map of Where Chips Get Made Is Quietly Shifting East.
articles.excerpt: Four new projects in Odisha, Punjab and Andhra take India's chip mission to 10 plants and Rs 1.6 lakh crore. For diaspora engineers, the question is whether the jobs follow the press releases.
articles.image_caption: A 200mm semiconductor wafer fabrication line, the kind of facility India is now building across multiple states
articles.nri_angle: For Indian-American chip engineers weighing a move home, the spread of fabs beyond Gujarat into Odisha, Punjab and Andhra is the first sign the semiconductor mission might create real careers, not just ribbon-cuttings.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Sundar Pichai Spent Three Years Being Called Late to AI. Google's Cloud Backlog Just Hit $460 Billion.
articles.excerpt: A near-doubling of signed cloud commitments in a single quarter is the clearest sign yet that Pichai's full-stack AI bet is paying off — and it reshapes the job math for Indians inside Google.
articles.image_caption: Alphabet and Google CEO Sundar Pichai
articles.nri_angle: For the thousands of Indian engineers at Google weighing AI-era job security, a $460 billion cloud backlog signals where the company is hiring and investing — and which teams are safest as the AI reorganisation grinds on.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Ola Electric Built India's Biggest Scooter Factory. Its Quieter Rival Is Opening a Store a Day.
articles.excerpt: As Ather expands toward 1,100 outlets and Ola shrinks from 4,000 to 700, India's electric-two-wheeler race has flipped from a land grab to a test of who can actually make money.
articles.image_caption: Ola Electric scooters, India's best-known electric two-wheeler brand
articles.nri_angle: NRI investors who bought into the India EV story through Ola's or Ather's listings now face a clearer divide: the flashy market-share leader is retreating while the disciplined rival expands, and the gap explains which bet is holding up.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Trillion Dollars Vanished From the Nasdaq in a Day. The Engineers Who Built the AI Boom Have the Most to Lose.
articles.excerpt: Tuesday's tech wreck wiped more than $1 trillion off the Nasdaq 100 as investors finally asked whether the debt-funded AI buildout can pay for itself. For Indian techies whose net worth, RSUs and job security ride on these stocks, the reckoning is personal.
articles.image_caption: The Nasdaq MarketSite in Times Square, New York
articles.nri_angle: Tens of thousands of Indian engineers at Nvidia, Google, Microsoft and Micron hold much of their compensation in the very AI stocks now in freefall — a correction that hits their RSUs, mortgages and visa-tethered job security harder than almost anyone.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Is Pouring Billions Into Deep Tech. Its Most Ambitious Founders Are Still Buying One-Way Tickets to America.
articles.excerpt: A 24-year-old Bengaluru founder building DNA-based data storage just shut her India operation to move to San Francisco — even as Premji Invest, Nvidia and Temasek shovel money into Indian deep tech. The contradiction is the whole story.
articles.image_caption: The Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru; India is investing billions in deep tech even as its founders head abroad
articles.nri_angle: The 'should I build in India or move to the Valley' question that has defined a generation of NRI founders is being answered in real time — and the answer reveals what the diaspora's home country still cannot offer its boldest builders.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Taxes Crypto at 30% and Calls It Compliance, Not a Ban. For NRIs Holding Bitcoin, the Fine Print Is Brutal.
articles.excerpt: Parliament has confirmed there is no plan to ban crypto — or to properly regulate it. Instead India runs a punishing tax-and-surveillance regime while betting its real money on UPI and the digital rupee. Diaspora investors are caught in the middle.
articles.image_caption: Physical representations of Bitcoin; India taxes crypto gains at a flat 30%
articles.nri_angle: NRIs who buy or transfer crypto involving Indian platforms or rupee accounts face a 30% tax, 1% TDS on every trade and new per-day penalties — while the diaspora's everyday money increasingly rides on the UPI rails New Delhi is promoting instead.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Accenture Just Had Its Worst Week on Record. The Fear Driving It Lands Hardest on Indian IT.
articles.excerpt: A cautious outlook and shrinking bookings wiped a quarter off Accenture's value. Wall Street is now treating the whole IT-services model — TCS, Infosys and Wipro included — as a thing AI might eat.
articles.image_caption: Accenture's office complex in Gachibowli, Hyderabad, one of its largest delivery hubs in India
articles.nri_angle: For the Indian engineer at a US IT-services firm and the NRI holding TCS or Infosys shares, Accenture's selloff is the clearest signal yet that AI is being priced as a threat to the entire outsourcing model, not a tailwind.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Tesla Now Has Five Showrooms in India and Almost No Sales. The Real Test Starts This Summer.
articles.excerpt: Hyderabad and Bengaluru just joined Mumbai and Delhi on Tesla's India map. But 100% import duties mean a Model Y costs nearly $70,000 — and only 350 have sold.
articles.image_caption: The 2026 Tesla Model Y, the company's lead model for the Indian market
articles.nri_angle: NRIs who own Tesla stock or are eyeing a move back to India get a live case study in whether a premium American brand can crack a price-obsessed market choked by import tariffs.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Adobe's Indian-Born CEO Spent 18 Years Building a Subscription Empire. On His Way Out, He's Tearing Up the Playbook.
articles.excerpt: Shantanu Narayen is leaving Adobe with a parting bet: give the AI tools away free, monetise later. Wall Street isn't sure his successor can pull it off.
articles.image_caption: Shantanu Narayen, the outgoing chief executive of Adobe Inc.
articles.nri_angle: Narayen is one of the original Indian-origin CEOs who made Silicon Valley's executive suite look like Hyderabad; how his AI-era succession plays out is a referendum on whether that generation's playbook survives the agentic shift.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Oracle Just Cut 21,000 Jobs in a Year — Its Biggest Purge Ever. The Filing Names AI as the Reason.
articles.excerpt: The database giant shed 13% of its workforce to bankroll a $70 billion AI data-centre spree. For Indian engineers on H-1B visas, the safe seat is now on the team building the machines, not maintaining the software.
articles.image_caption: Oracle's corporate headquarters towers in Redwood City, California
articles.nri_angle: Oracle's US and India campuses run heavily on Indian H-1B and L-1 talent, and the cuts hit legacy-software teams hardest while sparing AI and cloud — a stark signal for NRI engineers deciding where to sit.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Trump Wants a Working Quantum Computer by 2028 — Sooner Than IBM Plans One. Indian Talent Is Already in the Race.
articles.excerpt: Two executive orders fast-track a national quantum machine and an encryption overhaul. The funded workforce push is a hiring surge for exactly the STEM graduates the diaspora supplies — and India is running its own version.
articles.image_caption: An IBM quantum computer on display at a technology summit in Delhi
articles.nri_angle: Quantum sits at the physics-engineering-CS crossroads where Indian-origin researchers are heavily represented, and a federally funded workforce push plus India's own National Quantum Mission make this a two-country opportunity for NRIs.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's IT Giants Promised a Better Year in April. Three Months In, Analysts Already See FY27 Slipping.
articles.excerpt: AI automation and the West Asia war are squeezing TCS, Infosys, Wipro and peers, whose shares are down 30% in 2026. For NRIs, it's both a bruised portfolio and a worry about family inside the Bengaluru campuses.
articles.image_caption: The glass pyramid at the Infosys campus in Bengaluru, India
articles.nri_angle: Many NRIs hold Indian IT stocks directly and have relatives working inside these campuses, so the AI-driven squeeze on the $315 billion sector is at once a portfolio question and a family one.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Arvind Krishna Spent Years Calling IBM an AI Company. Now He's Buying OpenAI's Help to Prove It.
articles.excerpt: IBM joined OpenAI's cyber program and put a $5 billion bet behind securing the world's open-source code. For Indian engineers in security and consulting, it redraws where the jobs are.
articles.image_caption: IBM Chairman and CEO Arvind Krishna speaking at SXSW in 2025
articles.nri_angle: IBM's pivot to AI-driven application security reshapes the career math for the tens of thousands of Indian engineers in its security, consulting and Bengaluru delivery arms, even as CEO Arvind Krishna warns the broader AI buildout may be a bubble.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Every Tech CEO Is Pouring Billions Into AI Data Centres. The Founder of India's Biggest SaaS Firm Says He'll Sit It Out.
articles.excerpt: Sridhar Vembu calls the AI buildout a bubble, ships a made-in-India ERP, and rules out an IPO again. His pitch to NRIs is unusually direct: come home.
articles.image_caption: Zoho Corporation's headquarters in Chennai, India
articles.nri_angle: Zoho's bootstrapped, no-IPO, build-it-in-India playbook is a direct counter-pitch to the venture-and-equity model most NRI tech workers know, and Vembu is explicitly inviting Indian engineers abroad to return and build.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Washington Cut Off Anthropic's Best AI Models to Foreign Nationals Overnight. Indian Engineers Just Learned Who Owns the Switch.
articles.excerpt: A single export-control letter pulled Fable 5 and Mythos 5 from everyone, including Anthropic's own foreign-born staff. For India's AI workforce, the lesson is about dependence.
articles.image_caption: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei at TechCrunch Disrupt in 2023
articles.nri_angle: The export ban barred foreign nationals — a category that includes a large share of Indian engineers at US AI labs and the millions of Indian developers who build on frontier models — exposing how quickly access to critical AI can vanish.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Every Big Tech Firm Is Cutting H-1B Hiring. Nvidia Just Doubled Down — and Indians Are the Reason.
articles.excerpt: While Google and Amazon slashed visa sponsorships by up to 40%, Jensen Huang's chipmaker added certifications and pay packages that read like a different economy entirely.
articles.image_caption: Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, whose company expanded H-1B hiring while rivals pulled back
articles.nri_angle: For Indian engineers who hold roughly 71-73% of US H-1B visas, Nvidia's counter-cyclical hiring is the rare safe harbour in a market where a layoff now triggers a brutal 60-day deadline to find a new sponsor.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Forbes Just Named the 50 Hottest AI Startups. Six Are Run by Indian Americans.
articles.excerpt: From a cardiologist's medical-scribe tool to the open-source lab behind RedPajama, the diaspora's footprint on Forbes' AI 50 is no longer a curiosity — it's a pattern.
articles.image_caption: Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia (CC)
articles.nri_angle: For NRIs deciding whether to join a startup, fund one, or send a resume, the AI 50 is a map of where Indian-American founders are building the most fundable companies in the most competitive sector on earth.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk
